articles.title_zh: GM beats on Q3 results, tightens profit outlook, and unveils new $20 billion buyback
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
GM ( GM ) posted third quarter results before the bell that topped estimates, tightened its full-year profit outlook instead of boosting it, but issued shareholders a new $20 billion share repurchase program instead.
For the quarter, GM posted Q3 revenue of $50.0 billion, up 2.9% from a year ago and above the $48.52 billion Bloomberg consensus. GM posted adjusted EPS of $3.70 vs $3.57 estimated, with adjusted EBIT coming in at $4.1 billion, ahead of the $4.02 billion expected and up nearly 22%.
But the big update was guidance. For the full year, GM now expects:
Adjusted EBIT of $14.5 billion-$15.5 billion (prior $14.0 billion-$16.0 billion)
Adjusted EPS of $12.75-$13.75 (prior $12.00-$14.00)
Adjusted automotive free cash flow of $11.5 billion-$12.5 billion (prior $9.5 billion-$11.5 billion)
Investors were hoping for more, as the stock is getting hit in pre-market trade - down over 7%.
Both ranges keep the same midpoints as before — $15 billion and $13.25 — meaning GM trimmed the upside as much as the downside.
GM also lifted its adjusted automotive free cash flow forecast to $11.5 billion-$12.5 billion, from $9.5 billion-$11.5 billion.
GM's board approved a new $20 billion multiyear authorization with no expiration date. GM also declared a quarterly dividend of $0.18 per share.
"We think this is a proven strategy," GM CEO Mary Barra wrote in her letter to shareholders. "The new $20 billion multiyear share repurchase authorization we announced today further demonstrates our board's commitment to creating even greater shareholder value."
Barra also said GM is working to continue its momentum "despite growing inflationary pressures."
This is seen with GM's costs creeping up. GM now expects commodity inflation of about $2 billion (the top of its prior $1.5 billion-$2 billion range), including logistics and memory chip (DRAM) costs. It also cut its expected regulatory benefits to about $500 million from as much as $750 million. Offsetting that, gross tariff costs are tracking toward the low end of its $2.5 billion-$3.5 billion range.
Earlier this month, GM reported third quarter US sales of 670,974 vehicles , a drop of 5.5% compared to a year ago, as a collapse in EV sales offset gains from its pickups and small SUV s.
Based on GM's model-by-model figures, EV sales fell about 62% to roughly 25.5K units, shrinking to under 4% of GM's US volume from more than 9% a year ago. Excluding EVs, GM's sales were essentially flat, up 0.3%.
Sales of the Chevrolet Equinox EV plunged 92.4% to 1,905, the Blazer EV dropped 84.4%, the GMC Hummer EV slid 72.9%, and the Cadillac Lyriq fell 50.5%.
GM's gas-powered trucks helped deflect EV losses. Light-duty pickup sales rose 9.3%, led by a 13.3% jump in the Chevrolet Silverado light-duty to 100,221, while the GMC Sierra light-duty gained 2.9%. Heavy-duty models were softer, with the Silverado HD down 10.1% and the Sierra HD off 6.9%. GM said it is on track to lead the full-size pickup segment for a seventh straight year.

articles.title_orig: Lawmaker reportedly loses leg as car ramming stuns Australia
articles.title_zh: Lawmaker reportedly loses leg as car ramming stuns Australia
articles.content_orig:
Morning Rundown: Albertans vote to stay in Canada, Australian lawmaker reportedly loses leg in car ramming, and the dilemma stalking the Knicks’ title defense
An Australian lawmaker was in critical but stable condition Tuesday after being hit by a car in what authorities said was a deliberate attack, shocking a nation where political violence is extremely rare.
Helen Haines, a 65-year-old independent member of Parliament, was struck Monday by a white Toyota Land Cruiser outside her electoral district office in Wangaratta, a town of about 30,000 people in the southern Australian state of Victoria. She underwent surgery overnight after being airlifted to a hospital in the state capital of Melbourne, about 150 miles away.
Local media reported that one of Haines’s legs had been amputated and that she was fighting to keep her other leg. The Alfred Hospital in Melbourne did not respond to an NBC News request for comment on the reports.
Australian lawmaker in critical condition after car ramming
Police charged the driver, who they said was a 43-year-old local man, on Tuesday with intentionally causing serious injury, dangerous driving causing serious injury and causing harm to a federal official.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said earlier Tuesday that according to eyewitnesses, the driver had passed Haines and then performed a U-turn, hitting her as she was standing by the trunk of her parked car.
“It’s clear that there was a deliberate act here. This wasn’t an accident, someone, you know, just skidding off the road,” he told the Australian Broadcasting Corp., adding that the motivation was not yet clear.
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke told the ABC that witnesses had described seeing the driver reverse and then hit Haines a second time.
The suspect’s father said the family knew Haines well.
She was a “deeply respected, valued and much loved member of our local community,” Brendan Nugent’s father Rod Nugent and Rod’s partner Christine Cunningham said in a statement Tuesday.
“Helen has been our friend for more than 20 years and what happened to her yesterday is devastating and unfathomable,” the statement added.
Political violence is extremely rare in Australia , where lawmakers are often out in public with little or no security and their accessibility is a point of national pride.
“It’s an Australian tradition to have a chat to a politician that you bump into at the shops,” Josh Roose, an associate professor of politics at Deakin University in Melbourne, told NBC News in an interview.
But threats are rising as political rhetoric becomes more extreme, officials and experts say, particularly since the Covid-19 pandemic.
According to the Australian Federal Police, there were 1,067 incidents of threats, harassment, nuisance or offensive behavior against senior officeholders, parliamentarians and protected locations in the 2025-26 financial year, a 12% increase over the previous year and twice the number five years earlier.
In a 2023 study of Victoria state parliamentarians, 82% reported harassment and 85% reported threats of harm, said Josh Holloway, a senior lecturer in government at Flinders University in Adelaide, with female politicians more likely to face abuse.
Holloway said that Australian federal lawmakers, especially those in rural areas, typically work from “shopfront-style offices,” hold regular community meetings and attend local events without security.
Those practices may now come under scrutiny, “but reducing public access to their representatives can come with significant democratic cost,” he said in emailed comments.
Albanese said Tuesday that it was everyone’s responsibility to “turn the temperature down.”
“We can disagree with each other, but do it in a respectful way,” he told Australia’s “Today” show. “And that’s something that Helen Haines always was characterized by, was that respect that she showed to others right across the political spectrum.”
Albanese said later that he had spoken by phone with local barber Ricky Jefferies, who ran from his nearby shop to help detain Haines’s attacker in what Albanese said was “a great example of the Australian spirit.”
“I heard a loud bang, with no brakes. It was crazy,” Jefferies told reporters. “I just ran out the front to see what was happening.”
Jefferies, who said he removed a knife from the suspect’s pocket and pulled him out of the car, said a lot of people “just ran to help.”
Haines, a mother and grandmother who spent three decades working in rural health as a nurse and midwife and has a doctorate in childbirth, was first elected to Parliament in 2019, then re-elected in 2022 and 2025. Her family said in a statement that they were grateful for the “swift assistance of bystanders” as well as first responders.
The increase in political threats in Australia follows a similar trend in the United States and other liberal democracies, Roose said.
“Australia always echoes what we’re seeing internationally, but sometimes slightly behind,” he said.
Since the Covid-19 pandemic, there has emerged a “level of extremist discourse that is unparalleled in Australian history,” Roose said, one that is highly influenced by politics in the U.S.
Australia, and particularly Victoria, had some of the strictest pandemic lockdowns in the world, which left residents feeling  “imprisoned, but also disempowered,” he said.
Lingering feelings of resentment combined with the current high cost of housing, fuel and other necessities have contributed to a “deep hostility” toward the government, Roose said.
Politics in rural Australia, especially, have become “highly inflammatory,” he said, “because of the online space and the poverty and the desperation that, quite frankly, has seeped into these areas.”
Roose said the “paradox” was that the victim was Haines, who is not considered a polarizing figure and is “someone who’s grown up and spent most of their life in these regions.”
“It indicates, I suppose, the challenge facing democracies around the world,” he said.
Jennifer Jett is the Asia Digital Editor for NBC News, based in Hong Kong.

articles.title_orig: China defends DeepSeek after US ban of its AI from government systems
articles.title_zh: China defends DeepSeek after US ban of its AI from government systems

HONG KONG (AP) — China hit back Tuesday at a U.S. ban on Chinese artificial intelligence startup DeepSeek's products for federal civilian agencies, highlighting friction in the two AI powers’ heated technology race.
The agencies should remove DeepSeek and its affiliated products, as well as third party products and services developed using DeepSeek, from their IT systems, the Department of Homeland Security said in a notice made public on Monday.
The department’s order, dating back to late July, also blocks civilian agencies from procuring DeepSeek products and services. DeepSeek is one of China's leading and best-known AI companies and its open-source models are widely available in countries including the United States. They are mostly free to use.
The notice in the Federal Register alleges that DeepSeek’s models “present multiple threat vectors.” It said concerns include that its servers are located in China and that Chinese authorities' could potentially access private company infrastructure and sensitive U.S. data.
In Beijing, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said China will “will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies” when asked at a regular press conference about the U.S. ban.
“China consistently opposes the overstretching of the concept of national security and the politicizing of science, technology, economic and trade issues,” she told reporters at a routine briefing.
DeepSeek did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are set to meet in mid-November on the sidelines of the APEC, or Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, leaders’ summit in Shenzhen, China.
AI is expected to be on the agenda.
China and the U.S. have recently made progress in some collaboration on AI governance, including a U.S. proposal for setting up of a notification system on national security-related incidents, but the two countries are still at odds on many issues.
U.S.-led restrictions still ban China from accessing some of the world's most advanced AI chips and the machines that make them. Last week, Beijing rolled out new proposed plans to restrict exports of certain advanced AI models.
The U.S. has also said Chinese AI startups including DeepSeek engaged in large-scale “distillation,” or extraction of capabilities, from frontier American AI models, claims that Beijing has dismissed.
Earlier this year, the U.S. Federal Communications Commission announced it was barring imports of new foreign-made humanoid robots in a move seen as targeting China.

articles.title_orig: As Politicians Argue About China, US Patients Find Cutting-Edge Treatment There
articles.title_zh: As Politicians Argue About China, US Patients Find Cutting-Edge Treatment There
articles.content_orig:
Until recently, a Manhattanite might venture no more than a few dozen blocks to find the world’s most sophisticated cancer treatment. Cutting-edge American medicines have helped reduce the U.S. cancer death rate by about a third since 1990, and New York City hospitals deliver some of the best care in the country.
But in January 2025, the city’s health systems had no good options for Debbie Doppelt, a 60-year-old jeweler with an unusual form of lung cancer that mostly afflicts nonsmokers like her. The Food and Drug Administration hadn’t yet approved sunvozertinib, a drug developed in China that targets the mutation driving Doppelt’s tumors. She had been through chemotherapy and surgery, but the cancer had now spread to her brain. And she didn’t qualify for the relevant clinical trials.
Then an option emerged, in an offhand remark.
“Too bad she’s not Chinese,” a doctor told her son Max Doppelt, who had organized his mother’s care since her 2023 diagnosis. “She could go to a pharmacy in China and buy it.”
Within hours, mother and son had reached out to friends and relatives, one of whom procured a small supply of sunvozertinib from a contact living in China. A few months later, Max flew to Shanghai to get a refill.
Other patients have followed. “No organization or doctor is guiding patients to China, but word gets out,” Max said. He said he knows of at least 30 Americans who’ve made the pilgrimage to obtain the drug, which the FDA licensed in July 2025 but wasn’t yet on the U.S. market as of mid-October of this year.
Sunvozertinib, made by Shanghai-based Dizal Pharmaceutical, isn’t the only treatment drawing patients to China. Americans, Europeans, and others are trekking there to enter clinical trials for CAR-T therapy, an area in which China is now a world leader .
China, until recently known more as a supplier of drug precursor chemicals and generic medicines, has become a biotech powerhouse, accounting for as much as 46% of new drugs tested around the world in 2025. U.S. pharmaceutical companies are testing new therapies there and signing billion-dollar contracts with Chinese firms to develop and market their drugs.
China’s progress has alarmed some politicians, who warn of lost jobs and U.S. dependency on Chinese medicines. The Trump administration in June kicked off Operation TrialBlazer, aimed at speeding up some FDA regulatory processes to lure back more clinical trials.
China’s poor showing in vaccine and drug development during the covid pandemic prompted the country to overhaul its biotech sector, dramatically altering the global industry, said Sam Rasty, a veteran of small biotech companies who now leads one called FynderBio. Venture capital now flows heavily to early-stage clinical work in China and Australia, where regulatory systems enable key first-in-human studies much more quickly than in the United States.
Chinese companies are so much faster at this process that U.S. biotechs, which used to share early advances at conferences or funding meetings, now routinely conceal their progress out of fear that competitors will take their ideas and speed them to market, said Steve Potts, CEO of Breakthru Medicine, a small biotech.
At a meeting he attended in May, nearly all the 60 biotech CEOs in the room planned to run phase 1 trials in Australia, Europe, or China, Potts said. Five or 10 years ago, most of those trials would have been carried out in the U.S.
“Slow and prohibitive” FDA requirements are driving investment to more-nimble Chinese companies, President Donald Trump’s nominee to lead the agency, Heidi Overton, warned in her opening statement at her Sept. 24 confirmation hearing.
The movement of clinical trials overseas “should give pause to every American and those who serve on their behalf,” Overton said. “When we lose this advantage, we lose our health security. And when we lose our health security, we lose everything.”
Overton pledged to continue TrialBlazer, which mirrors Australian processes begun in 1991. It is aimed at accelerating clinical trials and approvals so patients do not feel compelled to seek treatment abroad, said Department of Health and Human Services spokesperson Emily Hilliard. It is sometimes legal to obtain medication abroad for personal use, but the FDA “cautions patients about potential safety and quality risks associated with treatments outside our regulatory system,” she added.
As the FDA moves to streamline drug development, members of Congress are trying to slow Chinese firms’ integration into U.S. biotech.
Rep. John Moolenaar (R-Mich.), who chairs the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, in June co-sponsored legislation with Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.) requiring all U.S. pharmaceutical deals with Chinese companies to be cleared by the Treasury Department.
Others see biotech protectionism as misguided. China’s focus on improved medicines can only help us, said Peter Kolchinsky, managing partner of RA Capital Management, which has Chinese investments in its biotech portfolio.
“We may be adversaries in many areas, but we’re not competing with them to cure cancer. We are collaborating with them to cure cancer,” he said. “There are things that are bigger enemies than any other nation on Earth.”

Cancer Knows No Boundaries
A minor but persistent cough led to the diagnosis of Debbie Doppelt’s cancer in late 2023. Chemo, immunotherapy, and surgery kept it at bay for months, but in December 2024, scans showed the cancer had spread to her brain, with 10 tiny tumors.
The FDA earlier that year had approved amivantamab, a drug that targeted the mutation driving Doppelt’s tumor, but Max was concerned about its toxicity. Also, several doctors he consulted told him that amivantamab might not penetrate brain tissue to fight cancer there.
Doppelt tried to enter a clinical trial at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, where she was a patient, for zipalertinib, another drug that targeted her mutation. But in January 2025, the Doppelts learned that a slight scarring on her lungs had rendered her ineligible for the study.
That left sunvozertinib, which gained approval in China in 2023. It was also being tested in the U.S., but only in late-stage trials in which half the subjects received chemotherapy only. That risk was a nonstarter for Doppelt, whose cancer had already outsmarted chemo.
So Max flew to Shanghai, returning with 26 boxes of sunvozertinib in his luggage. The drugs cost about $10,000, he said.
“Getting on the plane and bringing the medicine home felt like my life’s purpose,” Max said. “The data was so clear that this drug had significant efficacy in the brain. Anything else she might do, she might not last a year.”
On Sept. 1 of this year, AstraZeneca signed an agreement with Dizal to distribute the drug worldwide, and it plans to make it available in the U.S. by the start of 2027, spokesperson Tara Parsell said.
Doppelt, who runs a diamond business with her husband, has tried to stay positive and healthy, scarcely missing a day of work since her 2023 diagnosis. She said she’s grateful she has a loving community and the means to afford the best available therapies.
“I think I’ve been pretty successful at having, actually, an amazing three years,” she said. “In some ways a better three years, with all of it, than the three years before, because you’re so appreciative of everything.”
Doppelt’s parents were Holocaust survivors. “They were always saying: ‘This piece of bread tastes so good! Do you know what it is to be hungry?’”
Searching for help for his mother gave Max, a 30-year-old computer engineer, an idea for helping patients find the right treatment — which, in cases of advanced cancers, may be a clinical trial.
A year ago, he quit his tech job and started a company that uses artificial intelligence to combine data from research and drug company sites with a patient’s health records to help them find the right study.

articles.title_orig: Why are some food prices up and others down? Here are the stories of 5 items
articles.title_zh: Why are some food prices up and others down? Here are the stories of 5 items
articles.content_orig:
Ever since the pandemic, grocery prices have been out of whack.
COVID-related lockdowns forced people to eat at home more often, and in April 2020 grocery prices took their biggest leap in decades , increasing 2.6% from the month earlier.
Then, in 2022, food prices began another upward swing as Americans with cash on hand returned to stores in large numbers and retailers struggled to meet the pent-up demand. The food system faced other shocks that year, including a severe avian flu outbreak and Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Grocery prices rose 11.4% in 2022 alone.
That period of dramatic food inflation slowed down in 2023, though prices generally haven't returned to previous levels. Instead, grocery costs have continued to rise, just at a slower rate, roughly in line with overall inflation.
"But the damage had been done," said Ricky Volpe, a professor of agribusiness at Cal Poly San Luis Obispo. "Any inflation that happens now in the grocery store is on top of these already very high prices, and consumers are very sensitive to that."
President Trump pledged to lower grocery prices in his second term. And while some individual items have become cheaper since Trump returned to office, overall grocery prices are up on average. That has been driven by a number of systemwide factors, from increased labor costs to tariffs to higher energy prices caused by the war with Iran.
Zoom in on a single food item, though, and the story is often more complicated. Specific issues facing one crop, animal species or geographic region can influence the retail price halfway around the world. Sometimes, the price of an item swings far beyond what inflation itself can explain, or the price goes down when most other items are trending up.
We picked five everyday food items — ground beef, eggs, coffee, butter and chocolate chip cookies — to explain the complicated math behind what you pay in the grocery store checkout line.
The cost of ground beef has been on the rise for years, largely due to weather and financial pressures on producers. A typical pound of ground beef last month cost $6.79, an 85% jump from a decade earlier, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Recent droughts have devastated U.S. cattle herds, which can take years to recover. Layered onto that are the rising costs of farming equipment and fuel, a lack of land for grazing and a consolidated meatpacking industry that farmers and ranchers say eats into their profits. The number of U.S. cattle farms has been shrinking , according to the most recent Census of Agriculture. "I think there's still a sector of young people that have an interest in ag, but the barriers to entry to agriculture are huge," said Reid Hall, a Kentucky cattle farmer. All of that has led to the smallest U.S. cattle herd in 75 years.
The Trump administration has tried a number of measures to lower ground beef prices over the past two years, including allowing in more imports of ground beef with no tariffs. But U.S. ranchers have largely panned such moves, arguing that increasing the amount of imported ground beef will only make it harder — and more expensive — for U.S. farms and ranches to operate.
In recent years, the seesawing price of eggs has largely come down to avian flu , which affects wild birds and poultry. Large outbreaks force farms to cull their flocks to prevent the spread of the disease, diminishing the domestic supply of chickens and raising prices. That's what happened in 2022 and again in 2024, when there was a spike in the price of eggs, followed by a steep drop-off. How damaging avian flu is in a given season depends on the severity of the outbreak and the success of any biosecurity measures that U.S. farms take in response to the disease.
Outbreaks can have a whiplash effect on egg prices. An average dozen reached a record high of $6.23 in March of last year, when stocks were depleted by a brutal avian flu season. Yet last month, the typical U.S. price had dropped to $2.27 per dozen.
Though avian flu is the main driver of egg prices, it's not the only thing that can scramble U.S. poultry operations. The Trump administration's tariffs on foreign goods have also raised the cost of packaging materials , such as cardboard, that are used in egg cartons.
The U.S. imports more than 99% of the coffee it consumes. That was why the Trump administration's tariffs on countries like Brazil , which is responsible for 35% of the global coffee supply, were particularly bitter for U.S. coffee drinkers. Last fall, the Trump administration scrapped tariffs on some foreign goods in a bid to lower prices, and coffee made the list.
But the price of coffee last month was still 44% higher than it was two years before. Severe weather and climate change are jolting harvests. Both drought and heavy rainfall in coffee-producing countries such as Brazil, Vietnam and Costa Rica have ground down coffee bean yields. And excessive moisture on coffee farms can cause mold growth and disease.
Butter currently costs a lot less bread than it used to. A pound of butter averaged $3.96 in September. That was down 17.3% since last year, bucking the trend of rising food prices.
Interest in butter has spread recently, nourishing a strong demand for the dairy product. New dietary guidelines announced this year by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who spearheaded the Make America Healthy Again movement, encourage people to eat fats like butter.
Yet even though demand for butter is high, supply is even higher. U.S. butter production is booming, in part because dairy farms grew their herds and increased milk supply to produce more milk proteins for popular foods like Greek yogurt and cottage cheese. That has also led to an oversupply of butter.
The price of chocolate chip cookies began to rise steeply during the pandemic, hitting a record $5.35 per pound this January. (Last month, the classic treats were 20 cents cheaper.)
Part of the price spike can be explained by looking at the ingredients that go into chocolate chip cookies. The war in Ukraine ran up the cost of flour. Cocoa prices have hit multiple all-time highs in recent years. And avian flu largely determines what eggs go for in a given month. Some of those prices have come down recently, but the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported last year that baked goods have remained pricey in part because of a high consumer demand for "more expensive luxury treats."
Keegan Rodgers, founder and pastry chef at the Lakehouse Bakery in Chelsea, Mich., has resisted buying cheaper ingredients — such as margarine instead of butter — just to save money. "If I switched to garden-variety ingredients, my costs would decrease by about 30%," he said.
But Rodgers, who noted that he is also paying more for labor and insurance, said he has reluctantly raised his prices to be able to afford high-quality ingredients and employ skilled bakers. "Real food is more important than the bottom line," he said.

articles.title_orig: Review: Castlevania: Belmont's Curse (Switch) - A Pro-Grade Metroidvania With A Stiff Learning Curve
articles.title_zh: Review: Castlevania: Belmont's Curse (Switch) - A Pro-Grade Metroidvania With A Stiff Learning Curve
articles.content_orig:
What is a Castlevania game? Nothing but a miserable little melting pot of horror tropes drawn from famous literary archetypes—Carpathian gothica populated by Universal monsters and their lesser minions—with inspirations that run the gamut from Scandinavian folklore to Greek myth. Schematically, it is a series of platform-navigation sequences interspersed with combat encounters, levelling, magic, and weapon forging across a Metroid -inspired map.
Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is all of these things, and is therefore acceptable as part of the series’ evolution. Its basic tenet is live, die, repeat: becoming incrementally stronger until everything crumbles before your might. The rub, as it were, is that it so closely resembles a thousand other games that it needs to scream to be heard.
Some commentators have labelled it a generic work with a Castlevania skin, but I disagree: the format pioneered by Symphony of the Night remains a definitive throughline here. It’s got weaponry and magic, its narrative is canon, there are plenty of familiar faces, and its core is an assembly of platforming, whipping, and map exploration.
You play as Rose, the daughter of Trevor Belmont and Sypha Belnades (both hailing from Castlevania III ) as she sets out to rid Paris of a demonic besiegement.
Once off the boat and into the alleys, you find lanterns and candles that release RNG bonus icons when struck. Most drops are Mana meter refills for your secondary weapon, but life-ups and health potions crop up occasionally, too. Upon death you return to the last save room you passed, and these are placed intentionally, exasperatingly, far apart, requiring you to travel considerable distances without respite.
You start out doing what almost every Metroidvania has done for the last three decades: working your way across a map, filling it out via exploration, and noting impasses that require a specific skill to access.
The bar for challenge is drawn from the off: Belmont’s Curse is a professional-grade Metroidvania for Metroidvania experts. Grinding for levels and searching out attack and defence increases is key, and will make a notable difference when battling popcorn enemies. For bosses, though, the advantage is far less pronounced; levelling alone won’t let you sidestep having to learn evasive manoeuvres.
Belmont's Curse is probably the hardest Castlevania since Circle of the Moon , featuring a stiff learning curve, necessary grinding, and an absolutely enormous map to cover. And no spoilers, but you're never quite done when you think you are.
From the outset, simple archers carve chunks from your health, and even when employing a nimble range of evasive hops, backflips, counterattacks, slides, and combos, you still end up taking a beating. Enemies lack any hit-stun, meaning you can go toe-to-toe reeling off blows and they can just stand their ground and strike through. This will get on your nerves initially, but again, it’s an intentional and acceptable design decision that makes sense later on.
Everything up to the first boss fight is a concealed tutorial. Respawning is part of the order of things, and you had better get used to it. It takes around two to three hours (depending on skill level) before your respawn times begin to notably expand and your gains start to tip the scales in your favour. The first boss rodeo will see you ripped to shreds in 20 seconds, but it’s critical in getting you to understand the game’s demands.
On a side note, be sure to avoid the in-game difficulty slider. It’s a mystery why it’s even there, and comes with a warning that its usage may ruin the game: an outcome that is a mathematical certainty.
Belmont’s Revenge, you see, is 'good' challenging: a carefully constructed adventure that proves both rewarding and seductively compelling once you push beyond the initial hump. It's exciting and varied, testing you with surprise Kumite battles in ethereal arenas, or devilishly devised gauntlets teeming with giant saws, swing-hooks and decaying platforms.
A word to the wise: avoid the compulsion to go boss hunting. While the desire to beat the snot out of Joan of Arc is strong, the map is enormous, and it’s best to first etch out its distant reaches and increase your strength in the process.
The game’s new systems are mercifully simple to understand. Your magic meter allows you to use Arcana — or ranged secondary weapons — and refills are generous enough to encourage liberal use. With every boss you beat, a new Arcana is granted, along with additional abilities that expand both map and combat options.
There are weapon families to unlock: shields, fists, two-handed blades, etc., each able to increase in utility through four levels. Relics are your buffs, and you can apply a limited combination to Rose at any time, increasing attack power on a timer, defence, or even restoring health under certain conditions. Exploration is key to these acquisitions, and if needed, you can annotate the map with reminder icons.
It’s worth noting that the designers have done a painstakingly detailed job of the Paris layout. It’s a sprawling pit of fire and stone that ascends way up and way down, a dizzying clockwork machine of trapdoors, gates and bridges. It's wonderful to unravel, before it then unravels further.
The combat is a real highlight, pushing the series envelope. A blend of scrolling beat-'em-up commands wrapped in ninja-like agility, the pace of Rose’s movement and the breadth of her attack options is the game’s most addictive aspect. All of the weapons have a unique feel and learning curve, and, dare I say it, Belmont’s Curse has perhaps the most integrated and enjoyable whip usage of any Castlevania game. You use it constantly, swinging, sliding, and dashing from platform to parapet with a fluidity that resembles parkour.
The whip can also be used to hook onto enemies to cross chasms, or spring toward them and deal devastating mid-air uppercuts and aerial raves. Initially, you’ll be getting such a beatdown that little of this is doable, but give it time and you’ll be wiping the floor with much of the opposition, and looking good doing it.
Boss fights are dramatic, and later, spectacular, and come with genuine patterns to learn. That said, they do come off as frantic and a tad unrefined. Any telegraphing of attacks is unclear, and you tend to find yourself relying on brute strength to be the tipping point — which won’t often work reliably.
While the game’s combat flow and cadence is quite lovely, there are a few irritants. The loading times, at least on the Switch 1, are intrusive, and will have you grinding teeth when an enemy knocks you back through a door, or you accidentally reverse and have to wait through two loading screens just to get back to where you were. It’s not a dealbreaker, but it would have been nice if it were a tad faster and a tad less frequent. There are a few frame chugs here and there, too, and while you quickly stop noticing, you shouldn't expect it to maintain an unbroken 30fps on Switch (or 60fps on Switch 2).
The biggest argument one could lay at the feet of Belmont’s Revenge is that it does little truly original. Graphically it’s nicely done, like a parallax-layered painting, and has an atmospheric foreboding about its catacombs, dank districts, and Cemetery gardens — but it never really takes the breath away. Pixel art would have done the game some favours, and the sprite models, while serviceable, feel a little under-developed.
Musically, there are some nice harmonies and stirring motifs, but the classical grandeur of Castlevania IV , Symphony of the Night, and Rondo of Blood all overshadow the game’s rather uneventful score. Additionally, I found the English voice acting off-putting, with Rose phoning it in. Switching to Japanese audio helps considerably, and is delivered with the right level of energy.
Belmont’s Curse may not be wildly original, but its planning and execution are superb, its combat and whip-integration thrilling

articles.title_orig: GDC Festival of Gaming 2027 moves to four-day format to "create a higher quality, more focused and valuable experience"
articles.title_zh: GDC Festival of Gaming 2027 moves to four-day format to "create a higher quality, more focused and valuable experience"
articles.content_orig:
GDC Festival of Gaming will shift to a four-day format for its 2027 edition, taking place Monday through Thursday, March 1 to March 4.
Organisers stated that this change is "a deliberate step toward creating a higher quality, more focused and valuable experience" for attendees.
"Having explored the data and listened to our community, we're concentrating programming and opportunities during the days when the community is most active, while making it easier for attendees to balance their time at GDC with their professional and personal commitments."
"In 2027, expect robust conference programming, larger session rooms, more hands-on workshops, interactive experiences, and expanded networking over the four days."
The new Business Hall at Moscone West and all conference programming will be available throughout the four days. Festival Hall at Moscone South will operate from Tuesday to Thursday.
The addition of the Business Hall was announced earlier this year , along with new passes, enhancements to established programming such as the GDC Summit , and other schedule updates for 2027.
"We're always looking at how GDC can better serve the game industry, and listening to our community is a crucial part of that," GDC VP of content strategy Mark DeLoura previously explained to GamesIndustry.biz .
"After introducing the Festival of Gaming and making significant changes to the GDC experience in 2026, it was especially important that we listen closely to what worked, what could work better, and how people want to participate in GDC going forward."
DeLoura added: "GDC 2027 is about giving people more choices in how they participate at the show, making the week work better for the way the industry uses GDC today. The changes are about making the event more accessible, making it easier to make meaningful connections and accomplish what you came to GDC to do."
Yesterday, the Game Developers Choice Awards (GDCA) announced it will be accepting submissions from publishers and developers for the first time.
The GDCA previously used a nomination-based voting system through the International Choice Awards Network.
Games released on PC or console between January 1 and December 31, 2026 are eligible. The submission deadline is November 1, 2026.

articles.title_orig: France curfews calm unrest as Macron faces criticism over Gulf trip
articles.title_zh: France curfews calm unrest as Macron faces criticism over Gulf trip
articles.content_orig:
Curfews contributed to a "calm" night across France, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said Tuesday, even as public discontent remained high following the weekend's mass protests, looting and violent scenes .
Certain areas of several French cities were under curfew overnight, including Place de la République and Les Halles in Paris, and parts of central Lyon. Lille and Nice were among the cities to impose curfews for minors.
The unrest comes at a particularly fragile moment for France, where public anger over living costs and deteriorating services is colliding with political instability and a fiscal crisis that threatens to turn into a debt crisis as government borrowing costs rise to the highest level in decades.
The country faces a divided parliament with no majority and presidential elections in April 2027.
In a statement on Tuesday, Lecornu said local officials would impose new curfews where required.
Meanwhile, criticism is mounting over President Emmanuel Macron's decision to embark on a three-day tour of the Middle East as France suffers its most severe riots in many years.
Riots followed weeks of demonstrations over the country's education system , the cost of living and other issues.
While hundreds of thousands of people marched peacefully, pockets of violence erupted, shocking the country, as protesters smashed shopfronts and set Limoges Town Hall on fire.
Political commentator Christophe Barbier on radio station RTL said on Monday there was "no longer a pilot in the plane." At the same time, newspaper La Dépêche du Midi wrote in a scathing editorial that Macron had "to see if the misery of a reviled president is less painful in the Persian Gulf sun" as France "sinks deeper into crisis."
Macron said on Sunday he was looking to address high fuel prices and secure French energy supplies through the trip to Kuwait, the UAE, Bahrain and Qatar, while strengthening defense and security cooperation.
There is also public anger over claims that police lost control of the situation at the weekend as disorder and looting escalated. Police were earlier this month accused of excessive force in their response to student protests, after a 15-year-old ​boy's hand was blown off by a stun grenade.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez' offered to quit his post on Monday after claiming responsibility for what unfolded. Macron declined his resignation, saying immediate leadership of law enforcement was needed.
"The lack of enforcement means that more than 3,000 shops have been sacked, and for the economy today we awake with a feeling that the state cannot do the basic duty that it is supposed to do, and this is now creating somehow lack of trust," Fabrice Le Saché, vice president of business group MEDEF, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Tuesday.
"This is dangerous because we have been used to... riots in our country — remember the Yellow Vests and other movements — but this one has passed, I think, the level of the previous ones, and we cannot continue to keep going with that same type of situation every time we have social unrest," Le Saché said.
French businesses have one of the highest tax burdens in the euro area but now feel they cannot receive basic security in return, he added.
Lecornu said Monday that a support fund would be established for damaged or looted businesses, and that the government would talk with insurers to speed up assessments.
"The scale of the damage suggests this weekend's riots could ultimately prove more costly than the unrest that followed the death of Nahel Merzouk in 2023," which generated around 1 billion euros ($1.12 billion) in insured losses, Jess Middleton, senior Europe analyst at risk intelligence firm Verisk Maplecroft, said by email.
"Further violence is not inevitable, but protests linked to the underlying grievances, including cost-of-living pressures and discontent over public services and education, are likely to persist, putting continued pressure on the government to demonstrate that it can maintain order," Middleton said.
French markets came under pressure on Monday after the weekend scenes, with bonds, stocks and the euro all selling off, amid growing skepticism about the country's ability to bring down its deficit to a sustainable level.
Fierce debate is underway over the 2027 budget, with the government targeting an overall decline in the deficit to 5% of GDP from 5.4%.

articles.title_orig: United Airlines CEO: 'We should have a national wealth tax'
articles.title_zh: United Airlines CEO: 'We should have a national wealth tax'
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby gave a wide-ranging, often provocative interview to the New York Times, defending fees for aisle and window seats and countering the rise in airfares by asserting "it's expensive to fly airplanes."
"There are customers that pay more that get more," Kirby, 59, said in the interview that ran Oct. 18 .
But he struck a decidedly more populist note on the topic of wealth inequality — which he brought up when the Times asked him about waning trust in CEOs and his responsibility in dispelling it. Here's his full answer:
"Wealth inequality has become a danger to our society, and we need to address that," he said. "We should have a national wealth tax — it won't work by state because people will just move. And I think we should have inheritance taxes that get close to 100% at some level. I would pay them."
United Airlines stock rose 0.3% before the bell on Tuesday.
Kirby is not the first or only business titan to call for bigger taxes on the wealthiest Americans. Luminaries like Warren Buffett, Bill Gates, and George Soros have long advocated for increasing the tax burden at their rarefied wealth levels.
Read more: How much does a millionaire actually owe the IRS on tax day?
"We've updated our tax system before to keep up with changing times, and we need to do it again, starting with raising taxes on people like me," Gates wrote on his blog in 2020.
Marc Benioff, CEO of Salesforce ( CRM ), wrote in 2019 that "increasing taxes on high-income individuals like myself would help generate the trillions of dollars that we desperately need to improve education and healthcare and fight climate change."
Joe Biden was president, and Democrats in Congress were gearing up to pass legislation to tax unrealized gains on individuals with a net worth of at least $1 billion or annual income of $100 million for three consecutive years. Of course, that never happened, and after President Trump was reelected, Republicans in Congress passed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which included provisions that made lower marginal tax rates for high incomes permanent, along with other provisions benefiting wealthy Americans.
Read more: 10 ways the One Big Beautiful Bill Act affects student loans and financial aid
As for the inheritance taxes Kirby said he favors, there is no federal tax on individual beneficiaries of inherited assets. A few states impose a state inheritance tax.
There is a federal estate tax, but the exemption is so large — $15 million per person — that few people ever pay it. Only 0.2% of estates are large enough to be subject to the tax, and even then the tax applies only to the amount that exceeds the exemption threshold.

articles.title_orig: From France to Albania, social unrest is setting Europe’s streets ablaze
articles.title_zh: From France to Albania, social unrest is setting Europe’s streets ablaze
articles.content_orig:
Anger over the cost of living and pressure on public services has brought hundreds of thousands of protesters onto streets across several European countries, with grievances ranging from expensive housing to poor conditions in schools and universities.
France saw the largest demonstrations at the weekend, with more than 500,000 people marching. Most protested peacefully, but some looted and vandalized shops, set fire to city halls and attacked police officers.
Separate protests also took place in Italy, Spain, Portugal and Albania on Saturday and Sunday. Their immediate triggers differed, although high fuel and energy costs formed part of the backdrop in several countries. The wars in Iran and Ukraine have pushed diesel prices sharply higher across the continent.
There's no one "single trigger" for the riots, Capital Economics' Chief Europe Economist Andrew Kenningham told CNBC. The increase in energy costs may be playing a role, but the increase is smaller than in 2022, at the onset of the Russia-Ukraine war, when there were no comparable violent protests, he added.
Nevertheless, the demonstrations pose a shared challenge for governments: how to improve living conditions and maintain public services while supporting households and keeping strained public finances in check.
The demonstrations in France began last month when high school students criticized poor schooling conditions, including shoddy facilities and teacher shortages. They have since evolved into broader protests over living standards and declining public services.
In Spain, housing protests began in September after an 87-year-old woman, Maricarmen Abascal, was evicted following a 230% rent increase by an investment fund. She died a fortnight later.
Thousands of protesters also took to the streets in Portugal on Saturday to demonstrate against soaring housing costs and the cost of living.
"People obviously are protesting on the cost of living with diesel and fuel prices, but mainly on housing costs, which have been increasing substantially all over Europe, but also particularly in Portugal," Miranda Sarmento, Portugal's minister of state and finance, said Monday.
In Albania, protesters were angry about poor university conditions and high tuition fees, and called for the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama. Some threw Molotov cocktails and other objects at the police and set fire to cars and litter bins.
In Italy, a march in central Milan on Saturday over living costs also ended violently, with rioters attacking the police with stones and paving blocks and setting fire to barricades.
"The underlying problem is that politicians are not able to offer hope of a better life for many Europeans because the economy is growing only slowly and governments have built up huge debts, leaving them little scope to support higher public spending or to cut taxes," Capital Economics' Kenningham said.
The escalation of violence in France in particular is due to a "conjugation of different elements," said Douglas Yates, a professor at the American Graduate School in Paris.
"This was a storm that turned into a hurricane," Yates told CNBC's Steve Sedgwick. "There was this inflation, which has brought out the cost-of-living protesters who would have been disgruntled at any rate."
Yates said another factor is France's 2027 presidential election, as opposition parties seek to capitalize on growing public discontent with President Emmanuel Macron .
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has proposed a 2027 budget aimed at narrowing France's deficit , projected at 5.4% of gross domestic product this year. Measures include freezing the civil service pay index and tightening reimbursement for sick leave.
"Finally there's the students, the poor students who started this by making reasonable demands for having their dilapidated infrastructure repaired and perhaps getting some air conditioners installed in the classrooms, and so these three forces have come together and created an out-of-control hurricane," Yates added.
The economic backdrop has also deteriorated. In the second quarter of 2026, France's unemployment rate rose to 8.3%, representing 2.7 million people, according to Insee, the national statistics bureau . The unemployment rate among 15- to 24-year-olds climbed to 21.6%.
Consumer prices rose 3.1% in September from a year earlier, up from 2.4% in August, according to final Insee data. Energy prices jumped 21.3%. Meanwhile, purchasing power per consumption unit is projected to fall 0.7% in 2026, according to Insee figures, cited by Le Monde .
Calculations by the French Institute of Economics for Le Monde estimate that the decline in purchasing power since 2024 is equivalent to a loss of 1,200 euros ($1,345) a year for a household with two adults and two children, and 600 euros for a single adult.
Portugal's Sarmento said that the situation across Europe varies, with Portugal in a stronger fiscal position and with much less debt than France.
"Those countries [those with higher public debt] have much less fiscal margin to act, but the main issue is that we need to resolve the problem of productivity and competitiveness at the European level," he said.
"The European economy is not growing as much as the U.S., and without economic growth, it's impossible to have better salaries and to have the resources for better public services and social support," Sarmento added.
In the second quarter of 2026, Portugal recorded the EU's highest annual increase in house prices, up 16.5% from a year earlier, according to Eurostat .
The Portuguese government is looking to increase the supply of housing to reduce buying and renting costs to resolve the issue, according to Sarmento.
French government bond yields rose and the euro weakened on Monday as the unrest added to investor concerns over France's debt and budget.
"It will be difficult to see the budget deficit come down without painful measures," Sharon Bell, senior European equity strategist at Goldman Sachs, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Monday.
"Taxes could well go up for French businesses. I think taxes may generally go up in France. Fiscal consolidation means you need to either spend less or tax more. Those things are very tricky."
Mike Bell, head of market strategy at RBC BlueBay Asset Management, said France faced a "very real risk" of a sovereign debt crisis.
"What's needed in France is to get the fiscal position in order; they need to raise the retirement age — you can't retire at 62 if the average person's living to 84 — but if this is going on even before they start talking about that, then imagine what would happen on the streets of France if you tried to raise the retirement age... I mean, here in the U.K. it's 68," Bell added.

articles.title_orig: US bans govt agencies from using DeepSeek, China vows to protect firms
articles.title_zh: US bans govt agencies from using DeepSeek, China vows to protect firms
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration banned Chinese AI startup DeepSeek from civilian U.S. government agencies, citing security concerns.
The Department of Homeland Security on Monday made public the order requiring federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek-related technology from their IT systems and barring them from procuring DeepSeek products and services. The ban applies to federal civilian agency IT systems, including third-party products and services developed using the company's technology.
The move comes amid intensifying geopolitical tensions between Washington and Beijing, with artificial intelligence emerging as a key battleground in the two countries' race for technological dominance.
Asked about the U.S. move by Reuters, China's foreign ministry told the news agency that it would safeguard the rights and interests of its companies.
Mao Ning, a ministry spokesperson, said that "China consistently opposes the over-generalization of national security as well as the politicization of science, technology and trade issues," the agency reported.
The order, originally issued on July 24, applies to federal civilian agencies, including the Treasury, State and Justice departments, but it excludes the Department of Defense.
Since DeepSeek burst onto the scene at the start of 2025, several U.S. government agencies have imposed various restrictions.
Congress restricted the use of DeepSeek in intelligence community systems in December 2025. Earlier that year in March, U.S. Commerce Department bureaus told staff DeepSeek was banned on government devices, Reuters reported at the time. The Defense Information Systems Agency moved to block access to DeepSeek models in January 2025, according to reports from Bloomberg.
DeepSeek's AI models "present multiple threat vectors," the latest DHS order states, citing concerns over potential access to sensitive data by Chinese authorities and potential cybersecurity vulnerabilities.
The agency also warned that using DeepSeek's AI models could result in sensitive U.S. government data being transferred to China, potentially providing intelligence on American citizens and government programs.
The models may also contain malware or other security vulnerabilities, the agency said, citing open-source research that identified multiple critical vulnerabilities in DeepSeek's iOS app.
Executive agencies can request exceptions to the order, including delays in compliance, by submitting a written justification to the DHS within 60 days of the order's issuance.
DeepSeek and China's Embassy in the U.K. did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

Roland JUPITER-08 brings back the Boutique Jupiter-8 as a bi-timbral Synthesizer with up to 32 voices, built-in FXs, and a sequencer.
Ten years ago, Roland released the JP-08, one of the first synthesizers in its compact Boutique series—often called the “tweezers” series. However, this was discontinued a few years ago.
For the 45th anniversary of the legendary Jupiter-8, Roland reintroduces the Boutique Jupiter as the JUPITER-08.
The Jupiter-08 is the latest addition to the Roland Boutique series, marking the Jupiter’s return to the Boutique line—though not with an identical look or feature set.
The new version features an entirely new interface inspired by the original hardware. If you look more closely, you might think Roland had simply shrunk the original Jupiter-8—the interface looks that authentic.
The developers promise a hands-on experience without diving into menus. Numerous sliders and knobs let you access every feature of the sound engine. Speaking of the sound engine.
Like the previous JP-08, the new Boutique JUPITER-08 authentically emulates the legendary Roland Jupiter-8 Synthesizer. But unlike the former, the new one uses ABM (Analog Behavior Modeling), the same technology used in the Jupiter-X and Fantom-EX.
They chose ABM over ACB because it lets them offer much higher polyphony. According to Roland, the biggest customer request was to get more polyphony.
This change lets the new JUPITER-08 come in two parts , each with eight voices in the standard configuration . In a new advanced mode, you can max it out at 32 voices (16+16).
Small in size, each part still offers the classic JP-8 feature set: two multi-wave oscillators with cross-mod (FM), sync, and PWM; a 12 dB/24 dB resonant low-pass filter; a non-resonant high-pass filter; two envelopes (filter and amp); and a single multi-wave LFO.
The new Roland JUPITER-08 features refined voice allocation and pitch behavior that improve the analog recreation.
Additionally, you can now refine your sounds with a multi-FX processor with 17 unique effects , including chorus and MFX – plus dedicated delay and reverb with five types (shimmer mode…). These are designed for extensive sound shaping and spatial enhancement.
Each part also houses a 64-step polyphonic sequencer with up to 8 voices and motion recording to add a dynamic, evolving quality to your patterns. Also onboard is a multi-mode arpeggiator.
On the back, you have a power on/off switch, a USB-C port for data, power, and audio transfer, and a volume knob. The headphone socket, the main stereo output, and mix-in are all on 3.5mm stereo sockets. Plus, you have 5-pin MIDI IN and OUT.
Battery or USB-C power and built-in speakers make the Roland JUPITER-08 a very portable synth for on-the-go use.
This version includes a keyboard. More precisely, the K-25m keyboard dock makes the JUPITER-08 Boutique a standalone instrument.
The JP-08 was one of the most popular Boutique synths. It’s great to see it back in a more attractive and expanded version. I currently have the JUPITER-08 in for testing, and I “hopefully” will release a review sometime in October. Stay tuned!
The Roland JUPITER-08 is now available for $549.99/689€, including the K-25m keyboard.

articles.title_orig: China warns UK of ‘firm countermeasures’ if it joins EU import curbs on EVs
articles.title_zh: China warns UK of ‘firm countermeasures’ if it joins EU import curbs on EVs
articles.content_orig:
Beijing warns against ‘discriminatory’ step after France drops opposition to British role in Made in Europe package
No 10 has left the door open to imposing tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles as part of the Made in Europe package, prompting a warning from Beijing that such a move would be “discriminatory”.
Downing Street said on Friday that it would “welcome the objective to have the UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act” after France dropped its opposition to Britain joining the scheme .
The aim of the rules is to curb subsidised Chinese imports by giving EU-made products preferential treatment, but the UK and others such as Norway are worried about being left at a disadvantage if excluded from the scheme.
The price for joining would be aligning with the EU’s tariffs on Chinese EVs imposed by the bloc in 2024, according to a Franco-German proposal on Thursday night that said the UK would have to dynamically align with EU trade defence measures.
The Chinese embassy in London said it was “firmly opposed to any discriminatory practice involving tariff hikes or restrictive measures on Chinese products”. “We have expressed serious concern to the UK side regarding the reports in question,” it said, adding that “trade protectionism runs counter to WTO rules and market principles”.
This week, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said he would not be coerced into aligning with the EU’s policy.
However, the government has been desperate to be included in the Made in Europe package, fearing billions of pounds of trade in the car industry could be lost if the UK is locked out of supply chains in the EU.
Asked whether the UK accepted it would have to put tariffs on Chinese-made vehicles in order to join Made in Europe, a No 10 spokesperson said it was “premature to speculate” on the terms of any deal with the bloc and there was “still a European process to run”.
They added: “But more broadly, on the principle, the UK obviously has its own trade policy and it keeps all tariffs under review. And we work closely with the British automotive sector to make sure that that approach reflects their best interests.”
Chinese EVs are increasingly popular, with BYD sales up 78% year on year in September, Chery up 660% and the lesser-known Changan up by more than 3,000% in terms of market share.
EU lawmakers are expected to finalise the Industrial Accelerator Act, known as Made in Europe legislation, by the end of the year or early 2027.
But MEPs have already tabled 5,100 amendments, including one embracing the UK and giving Andy Burnham time to secure the deal he wants.
Earlier this week the boss of Mercedes-Benz, Ola Källenius, who is also the president of the European car trade body ACEA, warned that locking the UK out of legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc.
According to the new Franco-German proposal, there would be “an opt-in to further include European partners who were part of the EU single market as of 1 January 2020”, which includes the UK and Norway.
This would be provided those third countries accepted “dynamic alignment on the EU’s conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defence measures”.
Tariffs could help UK-based manufacturers by preventing cut-price Chinese models flooding the market but they could also push up prices for consumers and harm British manufacturers trying to sell vehicles to China in the case of an escalating trade war. About 80% of UK-made cars are exported, with more than half going to the EU and 6% to China.
Earlier on Thursday the trade minister, Anas Sarwar, hinted that the UK was minded to align on tariffs. He told Politico the UK and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to tackle China’s dominance in the automotive sector.
A car industry source said the EU “has recently shown that it is possible to have a dialogue with the Chinese and get some form of safeguarding in place” without retaliation.
China opposes the expansion of EV tariffs. In the past few months it has made what European Commission officials called “bloodcurdling threats” to launch a trade war over the latest plan to impose quotas on Chinese hybrid cars.
While quotas can be introduced within months under World Trade Organization rules, it could take more than a year to impose tariffs on Chinese cars, with strict processes to be followed, starting with notification of an investigation and followed by evidence-gathering and sharing over alleged harms China might be causing to the British car industry.
Liam Byrne, the Labour chair of the parliamentary business committee, has said imposing tariffs on Chinese EVs would be “a small price to pay” to save the industry in both the UK and the EU.
At a conference in London on Thursday night, he said the UK “urgently needs” a new strategy on China to ensure that British and European manufacturing “does not die”.
Byrne, who has been leading an investigation into the UK’s position on China, was highly critical of the government’s approach, which he believes is naive and based on false hopes that China will change its export policy.
“Our China strategy is simply not where it needs to be. The UK urgently needs a coherent China strategy, which it does not have today,” he said.

articles.title_orig: AI Fears Return With Data Center Firm Elice’s 33% Debut Flop
articles.title_zh: AI Fears Return With Data Center Firm Elice’s 33% Debut Flop
articles.content_orig:
Shares in South Korean AI services firm Elice Group plummeted 30% in their market debut on Tuesday, amid a sharp retreat in sentiment towards the sector that has also derailed other planned listings.
Elice, which raised 201.1 billion won ($150 million) in its IPO, provides AI cloud services as well as AI-based education and business software and plans to spend most of its IPO proceeds on launching portable modular data centers and related infrastructure.
Investors are increasingly questioning whether massive AI spending can pay off anytime soon as elevated inflation keeps borrowing costs high.
Analysts noted that Elice's IPO had been priced on Oct. 6, before the recent sell-off in AI-related stocks.
"Elice's debut shows the AI infrastructure trade has moved from 'build at any cost' to 'who is paying and for how long'," said Ke Yan, head of research at Singapore-based Shenton Research.
"Until the AI labs that rent ... capacity show they can fund their compute commitments, new listings across the region will likely be priced in that risk premium."
This month, data center firms that have shelved their IPO plans include Australia's Firmus, which is backed by Nvidia, Blackstone-backed AirTrunk, which postponed a Singapore REIT IPO, as well as SB Energy, a unit of Japanese tech investment conglomerate SoftBank, which had filed paperwork for a U.S. IPO.
"Everyone is not sure how much demand for AI there will be and it is hard to estimate current demand," added Kim Hak-joon, an analyst at Seoul-based Kiwoom Securities.
Elice's shares were last trading at 63,600 won compared with its IPO pricing of 90,500 won. The IPO drew institutional orders worth 388.84 times the shares available in the offering, according to a filing.
The company has said revenue for the first half of the year tripled to 34 billion won and that it swung to an operating profit of 10 billion won compared with a 3.5 billion won loss for the same period a year earlier.

United States Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during an undisclosed visit to Israel, according to Axios.

A spokesman for the US Department of Defense told Al Jazeera it “declines to comment” on the report.
Hegseth wrote on a social media post that he had visited US service members in the Central Command area of responsibility, which covers the Middle East, North Africa, and parts of Asia.
Israel’s Army Radio reported his meeting with Netanyahu took place at an air force base in Israel’s southern desert.
The reports of the visit come a day after President Trump took to his social media platform Truth Social to endorse Netanyahu in next week’s parliamentary election, the first vote since the Hamas-led October 7 attacks in 2023 and Israel’s genocidal campaign in Gaza.
Trump praised the prime minister for being an ally of the US in its war on Iran. He added that Netanyahu had his “Complete and Total Endorsement”.
“BIBI NETANYAHU WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!” Trump wrote.
Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist coalition is projected to lose its governing majority, although the opposition may also struggle to form a government, opinion polls suggest.
US Vice President JD Vance, however, declined to endorse Netanyahu in an interview earlier on Monday, saying he was not getting involved in Israeli elections.

articles.title_zh: What we know about Australian MP hit by car in apparent deliberate attack
articles.content_orig:
Australian independent MP Helen Haines is in hospital in a critical condition after she was struck by a car outside her electorate office in what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said appears to have been "a deliberate act".
The incident in Wangaratta, north-east of Melbourne, happened on Monday afternoon local time.
Albanese said counter-terrorism police are involved in the investigation.
Haines was struck by a White Toyota Landcruiser outside her electorate office on Monday.
The driver allegedly reversed to run into her a second time, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said.
"What witnesses have described is the driver doing a U-turn to get into the car park and to ram Helen against a vehicle, then to reverse and do it a second time," Burke told national broadcaster ABC on Tuesday morning.
A local barber Ricky Jefferies said he heard a loud commotion and ran towards the car, telling reporters on Tuesday that took a knife off the driver.
He said that multiple people "got involved immediately" to stop the alleged attacker.
Haines was airlifted to a Melbourne hospital where she underwent surgery.
She has lost one of her legs, according to local media. National broadcaster the Australian Broadcasting Corporation report that surgeons are working to save her other leg.
Victoria Police arrested the driver of the car, a 43-year-old man from the nearby town of Tarrawingee.
Local media reports have named the suspect as Brendan Nugent. Police have not confirmed the name of the man arrested.
Few details have been shared about Nugent, although he reportedly campaigned widely on environmental issues, including advocating against logging.
He was was detained at the scene by a passer-by before being taken into custody by officers, police said.
A knife was also seized, according to officers.
Victoria Police said it was unknown whether the suspect and Haines knew each other and its investigation remains ongoing.
On Tuesday morning Albanese said the suspect drove past Haines and did a U-turn "in order to get back" to where she was before hitting her with the car.
"It's clear this was a deliberate act," he told the ABC, adding it was not an "accident".
The motive for the attack is not clear, he said, and police are continuing their investigations.
Haines is a 65-year-old Independent MP for the Indi division in Victoria, south-eastern Australia.
She grew up in the south west of Victoria on a dairy farm with four brothers before training as a nurse and a midwife.
She became the matron of the Chiltern Bush Nursing Hospital in Victoria when she was 26, before later completing a master's degree in public health and a PhD in Medical Science while raising her three children and working, according to her website. She lives with her family on a small cattle farm outside Wangaratta.
The MP was first elected to the Australian House of Representatives in 2019 and was re-elected in 2022 and 2025.
Haines's family said the incident happened outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, a city of about 30,000 people, a few hours north-east of Melbourne in the state of Victoria.
Police said she was hit outside an office on Murphy Street at about 15:35 local time (05:35 BST).
Albanese appeared close to tears during a live television interview on ABC's 7.30 programme when he was asked if Australian politicians talk among themselves about the threats and risks they face.
"Yes," he replied, adding: "My concern at this point in time is for one of my colleagues."
He later described how there had been a "rise in temperature" and "too much shouting, not enough discourse" in Australia.
Speaking in a news conference, Australian Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said there had been an increase in reports of harassing and threatening behaviour towards lawmakers in the 2025-26 financial year, compared with 951 for the previous year.
Paying tribute to Haines during a news conference, Albanese described her as "incredibly hard-working".
"She is fiercely intelligent but most importantly she is just a thoroughly decent human being full of integrity and respected right across the Parliament and from everyone who comes into contact with her", he added.
He said the attack will come as an "incredible shock" to her community.
Australia's Foreign Minister Penny Wong described the incident as a "shocking and deeply disturbing attack".
The Premier of Victoria Ben Carroll said he was "deeply appalled" by the "violent attack".
Meanwhile, Australia's opposition leader Angus Taylor said he was "deeply saddened and distressed" by the attack.
"This is a shocking day for our nation," he said. "No-one should be targeted in this way."
But MPs from a range of political backgrounds have also described feeling deeply concerned about their safety in recent times: wearing disguises in public, locking their office doors, and scanning every crowd for potential threats.

articles.title_zh: An AI bust could come from places investors aren't watching, an economist says
articles.content_orig:
As concerns about an AI bubble mount, an economist is warning that investors may be overlooking other vulnerabilities in the boom.
"The trigger doesn't have to be endogenous to the boom. It could be external," wrote Dario Perkins, managing director of global macro at Global Data.TS Lombard, in a note on Monday.
Perkins argues that much of the industry's revenue growth still comes from spending within the AI ecosystem rather than businesses and consumers paying for AI services.
"The question is whether those revenues are coming from businesses and end-users outside the ecosystem — presumably to pay for productivity-enhancing tools — or from simple capex recycling," he wrote.
The warning comes after a recent chip-stocks selloff that has intensified concerns about whether massive AI infrastructure spending will pay off.
Last week, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell more than 11% before clawing back 2% on Monday.
One potential fault line is debt outside Big Tech.
While hyperscalers such as Microsoft, Amazon, and Google have strong balance sheets, smaller cloud providers, model developers, and infrastructure suppliers have been taking on increasing leverage.
Perkins estimates that debt across parts of the AI ecosystem could reach $2 trillion by the end of 2027.

He doesn't see AI-related debt as a systemic financial risk, but warned that earnings disappointments and canceled orders could ripple across the ecosystem. Even cash-rich hyperscalers could decide not to renew data center leases, leaving weaker companies exposed.
Another risk is an unexpected chip glut, as companies reportedly over-order semiconductors to guard against shortages, potentially creating excess supply if demand slows.
"Let's not forget we are talking about tech hardware and chips, notoriously cyclical, and prone to bullwhip effects," Perkins wrote.
Higher interest rates could further undermine the economics of AI investment, particularly for companies reliant on borrowing to finance their expansion.
But Perkins sees another potential trigger that has little to do with corporate earnings: political backlash.
"AI boosters on social media live in a bubble," Perkins wrote.
"They don't realize that ordinary people don't like AI. They don't find it useful, they REALLY don't want to live near datacenters, and they are worried about their jobs. And they vote," he added.
Perkins suggested that a single high-profile incident could rapidly turn that unease into broader opposition.
"One high-profile accident turns AI toxic," he wrote.

articles.title_orig: Drone strike in disputed Sudan-South Sudan area kills dozens, minister says
articles.title_zh: Drone strike in disputed Sudan-South Sudan area kills dozens, minister says
articles.content_orig:
Witness says drone struck twice at transport hub in al-Dibab, in one of deadliest single attacks of war
A drone strike near a market in southern Sudan on Sunday evening killed 80 people, mostly commuters catching rides home.
Ahmed Wadi, a witness, said the attack in the town of al-Dibab in West Kordofan state left “50 bodies who I helped bury, one of them my own brother Mohamed”.
Using a satellite internet connection to circumvent a communications blackout, Wadi also said 47 other people were transported to the nearest town, al-Mujlad. A medical source, requesting anonymity for his safety, said 30 of them died from their injuries.
The medic said: “A total of 80 people were killed in the drone strike on al-Dibab, and another drone strike on al-Mujlad injured four who are currently being treated.”
Wadi said the drone struck twice, 10 minutes apart, “on a transport hub where people gather to travel back to their villages after the market day ends”.
The attack is one of the deadliest single strikes since war broke out in April 2023 when a power struggle between the Sudanese armed forces (SAF), headed by Gen Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo , erupted into violence in the capital, Khartoum.
The RSF-declared administration, known as Tasis, accused the army of carrying out Sunday’s strike. All of West Kordofan state is under RSF control.
Sudan has witnessed an escalation in the use of drones in the war. Between January and April, drone strikes accounted for at least 880 civilian deaths, more than 80% of all conflict-related civilian deaths in Sudan.
After drone strikes on a busy livestock market in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur state, on Friday, the SAF said they had killed RSF fighters, but the RSF accused the military of killing 30 civilians.
The fighting in Sudan has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced many more. It has been fuelled by foreign powers with vested interests who are supporting sides in the conflict.
Last week, Rosemary DiCarlo, the undersecretary-general for political and peacebuilding affairs at the UN, warned the security council that the conflict and humanitarian crisis was deteriorating “with no breakthrough on the horizon”.
She said: “They [the warring parties] are not moving closer to dialogue. On the contrary, they seem to believe that they can make greater gains on the battlefield and that continued external support will allow them to pursue their objectives by force.”
AFP contributed to this report
